10.1 — Comparing pig housing systems
Theory
Understand the idea

Pig housing systems can be compared by using the same criteria for each system rather than deciding which one is best before examining the evidence. Broad examples include indoor, deep-litter, free-range and outdoor-bred arrangements. These labels describe general production systems, but individual farms may organise and manage them in different ways.

Shelter and outdoor access are useful comparison criteria. Indoor systems provide shelter throughout production, while free-range systems include outdoor access. Outdoor-bred systems involve pigs being born outdoors before later production stages may occur under different arrangements. Deep-litter systems use bedding material on the floor of sheltered housing. These descriptions explain general features but do not describe every individual enterprise.

Other useful criteria include bedding, space and land requirements, environmental control, exposure to weather or predators, monitoring, waste or land management and biosecurity. Environmental control may be easier in some sheltered systems, while outdoor systems may involve greater exposure to changing weather conditions. Waste and land management requirements also differ between systems because production environments are organised differently.

Monitoring is important in every housing system. Farmers observe animal condition, facilities and environmental conditions so they can make informed management decisions. Biosecurity also remains important because reducing the risk of disease introduction and spread requires planning and controlled management regardless of the housing arrangement.

Students should compare systems by applying the same questions to each one. For example, they can ask how shelter is provided, whether bedding is used, how weather exposure is managed, what monitoring is required and how waste or land is managed. Using consistent criteria helps produce a fair comparison.

Photographs can provide evidence about visible features such as fencing, shelter or bedding. However, a photograph alone cannot prove the complete housing system, management practices or animal welfare outcomes. A defensible conclusion combines visible observations with reliable supporting information and avoids claiming that one housing system is automatically best.

Key takeaways

Pig housing systems should be compared using the same criteria for each arrangement.

Useful comparison criteria include shelter, outdoor access, bedding, environmental control, monitoring, waste management and biosecurity.

Photographs show visible features but cannot prove the whole housing system or welfare outcomes.

A fair comparison uses evidence and avoids assuming one system is automatically best.

Knowledge check

What is the best way to compare pig housing systems?
A. Apply the same criteria to each system
B. Choose a favourite system first
C. Compare only one visible feature
D. Assume one system is always best

Answer: A. Apply the same criteria to each system
Correct feedback: Correct. Fair comparisons use the same criteria for every housing system.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph explaining how housing systems should be compared.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which housing arrangement commonly uses bedding on the floor of sheltered housing?
A. Deep-litter
B. Free-range
C. Outdoor-bred
D. Broad indoor

Answer: A. Deep-litter
Correct feedback: Correct. Deep-litter systems use bedding material within sheltered housing.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Look at the paragraph describing the general features of each housing arrangement.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which statement about free-range systems is supported by the theory?
A. They include outdoor access
B. They never use shelter
C. They eliminate monitoring
D. They guarantee better welfare

Answer: A. They include outdoor access
Correct feedback: Correct. Free-range systems include outdoor access, but no universal claims are made about outcomes.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory describes outdoor access but avoids absolute claims.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

What does the term outdoor-bred describe?
A. Pigs born outdoors before later production may occur under different arrangements
B. Pigs that remain outdoors for every stage of life
C. A system with no shelter
D. A guarantee of one management method

Answer: A. Pigs born outdoors before later production may occur under different arrangements
Correct feedback: Correct. Outdoor-bred refers to pigs being born outdoors, with later stages possibly occurring under different arrangements.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph explaining the meaning of outdoor-bred.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which is a useful comparison criterion?
A. Environmental control
B. Package colour
C. Farm logo
D. Advertising style

Answer: A. Environmental control
Correct feedback: Correct. Environmental control is one of the criteria used to compare housing systems.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Choose a factor directly related to how pigs are housed and managed.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Why is monitoring important in every housing system?
A. It supports informed management decisions
B. It removes the need for planning
C. It guarantees identical outcomes
D. It replaces biosecurity

Answer: A. It supports informed management decisions
Correct feedback: Correct. Monitoring provides evidence that supports management decisions.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph explaining the role of monitoring.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

What is the purpose of biosecurity?
A. To reduce the risk of disease introduction and spread
B. To guarantee production success
C. To replace environmental management
D. To identify housing systems from photographs

Answer: A. To reduce the risk of disease introduction and spread
Correct feedback: Correct. Biosecurity aims to reduce the risk of disease entering or spreading within production systems.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Focus on the purpose of biosecurity rather than overall production outcomes.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Why do waste or land management requirements differ between systems?
A. Production environments are organised differently
B. Every farm uses identical layouts
C. Weather has no influence
D. All housing systems produce the same conditions

Answer: A. Production environments are organised differently
Correct feedback: Correct. Different housing arrangements create different management requirements.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph comparing waste and land management.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

What can a photograph reliably show?
A. Visible features such as shelter or bedding
B. Overall animal welfare outcomes
C. Complete management practices
D. The full housing system in every detail

Answer: A. Visible features such as shelter or bedding
Correct feedback: Correct. A photograph can show visible features but not the entire production system.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Think about the difference between visible observations and conclusions about management.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which conclusion is best supported by the theory?
A. Housing systems should be judged using evidence rather than automatic rankings
B. One housing system is always the best choice
C. A photograph proves animal welfare outcomes
D. Outdoor access alone determines suitability

Answer: A. Housing systems should be judged using evidence rather than automatic rankings
Correct feedback: Correct. Strong conclusions compare evidence across common criteria and avoid universal rankings.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the final paragraph about evidence and the limits of photographs.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Written evidence

Prompt: Compare two pig housing systems using four common criteria from the theory and explain one difference for each criterion.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: An indoor system provides shelter throughout production, while a free-range system includes outdoor access. Deep-litter systems use bedding, whereas bedding arrangements may differ in other systems. Environmental control and weather exposure can also differ. The comparison uses the same criteria for both systems without claiming one is automatically better.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Prompt: Explain why a photograph cannot prove a pig housing system or its welfare outcomes.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: A photograph can show visible features such as fencing, shelter or bedding, but it cannot reveal the full management system, monitoring practices, biosecurity arrangements or welfare outcomes over time. Reliable conclusions require additional evidence from trustworthy information and consistent comparison criteria.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Pig housing: https://australianpork.com.au/about-pig-farming/housing; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Source boundary

Teach  pig housing systems by comparing common criteria and evidence. Do not ask students to identify systems from photographs, repeat activity image answers, provide stocking figures or make universal welfare rankings. Any practical observations or local production examples should be confirmed by the teacher.

Sources

10.2 — Feed, growth and production goals
Theory
Understand the idea

Pig nutrition involves supplying a balanced diet that supports growth, health and the intended production goal. A balanced diet provides energy, protein and amino acids, minerals, vitamins, fibre and water. These parts work together, so one ingredient alone does not provide everything a pig needs.

Grains can be important energy sources, but grains by themselves do not form a complete balanced diet. Other nutrients are needed to support body growth, tissue development and normal body functions. Water is also essential and must be considered as part of the overall nutrition system rather than as a separate extra.

Nutrient needs can change with life stage, health, environmental conditions and production goals. A younger animal may have different nutritional requirements from a mature animal. Conditions such as heat, cold or illness may also affect needs and performance. For this reason, a feeding approach should not be assumed to suit every pig or every situation.

Production goals may include supporting steady growth, reproduction, maintenance or particular product outcomes. These goals influence which records are useful when evaluating the system. Records may include feed supplied, growth measurements, health observations and changes in environmental conditions. Records help identify patterns and allow decisions to be based on evidence rather than guesses.

Feed conversion describes the relationship between the amount of feed used and the growth produced. It is a way of evaluating how effectively feed is being converted into body growth. A feed-conversion result should not be judged alone because growth can also be influenced by genetics, health, environment and management.

Students should understand the concepts of balanced nutrition, changing needs, production goals and record-based evaluation. They should not design feed formulas, calculate feeding quantities, diagnose health problems or provide animal-care instructions. These decisions require current specialist knowledge and controlled management.

Key takeaways

Balanced pig diets provide energy, protein and amino acids, minerals, vitamins, fibre and water.

Grains may supply energy but do not provide a complete balanced diet by themselves.

Nutritional needs change with life stage, health, environment and production goals.

Feed and growth records help evaluate performance using evidence rather than assumptions.

Knowledge check

What is the main purpose of a balanced pig diet?
A. To supply a range of nutrients needed for growth and health
B. To provide energy from grain only
C. To make every pig grow at the same rate
D. To remove the need for water

Answer: A. To supply a range of nutrients needed for growth and health
Correct feedback: Correct. A balanced diet supplies several nutrients that work together to support growth, health and production goals.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph and identify the range of nutrients required.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Which nutrient group helps supply energy in a pig diet?
A. Grains may contribute energy
B. Minerals are the only energy source
C. Water provides all dietary energy
D. Vitamins replace all feed ingredients

Answer: A. Grains may contribute energy
Correct feedback: Correct. Grains may provide energy as one part of a balanced diet.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory explains that grains can supply energy but are not a complete diet.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Why are grains alone not a complete pig diet?
A. Pigs also require protein, amino acids, minerals, vitamins, fibre and water
B. Grains contain no energy
C. Pigs require only water and fibre
D. Every grain has identical nutrient content

Answer: A. Pigs also require protein, amino acids, minerals, vitamins, fibre and water
Correct feedback: Correct. A complete diet requires several nutrient groups, not just an energy source.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the first two paragraphs and identify what grains do not supply by themselves.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Why is water included in the nutrition system?
A. It is essential for normal body functions
B. It replaces protein and minerals
C. It is needed only during hot weather
D. It guarantees rapid growth

Answer: A. It is essential for normal body functions
Correct feedback: Correct. Water is an essential part of overall nutrition and normal body function.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. The theory treats water as an essential nutrient, not an optional extra.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Why might a young pig have different nutritional needs from a mature pig?
A. Nutrient needs change with life stage
B. All pigs require identical diets
C. Age affects only coat colour
D. Mature pigs no longer require nutrients

Answer: A. Nutrient needs change with life stage
Correct feedback: Correct. Life stage influences nutrient requirements and production needs.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph explaining how needs change with life stage.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Which factor can affect a pig's nutritional needs?
A. Environmental conditions
B. Package design
C. Retail advertising
D. Breed photograph alone

Answer: A. Environmental conditions
Correct feedback: Correct. Environmental conditions can affect needs and performance.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Choose a factor linked directly to the animal and its production environment.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

What is feed conversion?
A. The relationship between feed used and growth produced
B. The process of turning grain into water
C. A method of identifying pig breeds
D. A record of transport distance

Answer: A. The relationship between feed used and growth produced
Correct feedback: Correct. Feed conversion compares feed input with growth output.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the paragraph defining the relationship between feed and growth.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Why should feed conversion not be judged by itself?
A. Growth is also affected by genetics, health, environment and management
B. Feed conversion always proves health
C. It measures only water intake
D. It guarantees the production goal was achieved

Answer: A. Growth is also affected by genetics, health, environment and management
Correct feedback: Correct. Other factors can influence growth and must be considered with feed-conversion records.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Look at the factors listed after the feed-conversion definition.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

How do records support production decisions?
A. They show patterns in feed, growth, health and conditions
B. They guarantee every decision is correct
C. They replace monitoring
D. They remove all uncertainty

Answer: A. They show patterns in feed, growth, health and conditions
Correct feedback: Correct. Records provide evidence that can reveal patterns and support informed decisions.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Records support evaluation, but they do not guarantee outcomes or replace monitoring.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Which task is appropriate for students in this section?
A. Explain how balanced diets and records support production goals
B. Design an exact feed formulation
C. Diagnose a pig's health condition
D. Set a feeding schedule for a farm

Answer: A. Explain how balanced diets and records support production goals
Correct feedback: Correct. Students should explain the concepts without giving operational or medical instructions.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the final paragraph, which sets the boundary between conceptual learning and specialist decisions.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Written evidence

Prompt: Explain why grain alone does not provide a complete balanced diet for pigs and name four other required components.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Grain may provide energy, but pigs also require protein and amino acids, minerals, vitamins, fibre and water. These nutrients support growth, tissue development and normal body functions, so one ingredient alone cannot provide a complete balanced diet.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Prompt: Explain how feed, growth and health records can be used to evaluate a production goal.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: Records can show how much feed was supplied, how growth changed and whether health or environmental conditions also changed. These patterns help evaluate whether the production goal is being supported. Feed conversion can be considered, but it should be interpreted with genetics, health, environment and management evidence.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Pork — Industry education information: https://australianpork.com.au/

Source boundary

Teach  balanced nutrition, changing nutrient needs, production goals, feed conversion and record-based evaluation conceptually. Do not provide feed formulations, quantities, schedules, weight categories, medication, diagnosis, animal-care instructions or local feeding procedures.

10.3 — Welfare evidence and defensible choices
Theory
Understand the idea

Animal welfare is an outcome that should be assessed using several types of evidence rather than one photograph, label or housing feature. Useful evidence includes animal-based indicators and resource or management indicators.

Animal-based indicators focus on the animals themselves. Examples include behaviour, health observations, injury evidence and signs of thermal comfort or discomfort. These observations can help show how animals are responding to their environment, but one observation at one moment may not represent conditions over time.

Resource and management indicators examine what is provided and how the system is managed. Examples include access to feed and water, housing condition, shelter, monitoring practices and reliable records. These indicators are important, but the presence of a resource alone does not prove a successful welfare outcome. Evidence should connect what was provided with observations of the animals.

Production choices can involve trade-offs among welfare, biosecurity, land use, cost, environmental management, monitoring and production goals. For example, one arrangement may provide greater environmental control but require more infrastructure and waste management. Another may provide greater outdoor access but involve increased exposure to weather or other site-specific risks. A trade-off is not automatically good or bad; its importance depends on evidence and context.

A defensible choice applies the same criteria to each option, cites relevant evidence, acknowledges uncertainty and avoids claiming that one system is universally best. Records collected over time are usually stronger evidence than a single image or unsupported statement.

In Australia, animal-welfare law is primarily the responsibility of state and territory governments. The current national government table lists the 2008 Model Code of Practice for the Welfare of Animals: Pigs. However, the legal requirements applying in a particular place must be confirmed from current state or territory sources. This lesson supports conceptual comparison only and does not provide local procedures or authorise practical animal-use activities.

Key takeaways

Animal welfare is assessed using multiple animal-based and resource or management indicators.

The presence of housing, feed or water alone does not prove a successful welfare outcome.

Production decisions may involve trade-offs among welfare, biosecurity, land, cost, environment and production goals.

Defensible choices use common criteria, supporting evidence and cautious conclusions.

Knowledge check

Why should animal welfare be assessed using several indicators?
A. One observation or resource cannot show the complete welfare outcome
B. Every indicator always gives the same result
C. A photograph proves conditions over time
D. Housing type alone determines welfare

Answer: A. One observation or resource cannot show the complete welfare outcome
Correct feedback: Correct. Multiple indicators provide a stronger picture than one observation, resource or image.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Review the opening paragraph and consider why one type of evidence may be incomplete.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal Welfare Standards and Guidelines: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/standards-guidelines; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which is an animal-based welfare indicator?
A. Observed behaviour
B. Building cost
C. Land area
D. A product label

Answer: A. Observed behaviour
Correct feedback: Correct. Behaviour provides evidence about how animals are responding to their conditions.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Animal-based indicators focus directly on the animals rather than business or property features.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal Welfare Standards and Guidelines: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/standards-guidelines; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which observation may provide evidence about animal welfare?
A. Signs of injury
B. The colour of farm advertising
C. The product's retail price
D. The name of the housing system

Answer: A. Signs of injury
Correct feedback: Correct. Injury evidence is one animal-based indicator that may help assess welfare.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Choose evidence that directly relates to the animal's physical condition.
Source: Authorised Module 10 lesson: https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1y9UkymrFNbfa8ZyU_qRp_jnz34mSY7wuyGWxCEdBAjM/edit; Australian Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal Welfare Standards and Guidelines: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/standards-guidelines; Australian  Government Department of Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry — Animal welfare in Australia: https://www.agriculture.gov.au/agriculture-land/animal/welfare/animal-welfare-in-australia

Which is a resource or management indicator?
A. Access to feed and water
B. A universal welfare ranking
C. The popularity of a system
D. A photograph without context

Answer: A. Access to feed and water
Correct feedback: Correct. Access to feed and water is a resource indicator used within welfare assessment.
Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Resource indicators examine what is provided within the managed system.

What is a trade-off in a production decision?
A. A benefit in one area accompanied by a cost or limitation in another
B. A choice with no disadvantages
C. A claim that every system is identical
D. A decision made without criteria

Answer: A. A benefit in one area accompanied by a cost or limitation in another
Correct feedback: Correct. Trade-offs involve advantages in some criteria and costs or limitations in others.

A. They can show patterns and changes across a longer period

A. Applying the same criteria and citing relevant evidence

A. Available evidence may not prove every condition or future outcome

Incorrect feedback: Not quite. Strong conclusions distinguish supported findings from what remains unknown.

Written evidence

Prompt: Compare two pig-production arrangements using four welfare indicators and identify one trade-off without declaring either system universally best.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: The arrangements could be compared using behaviour, injury evidence, access to feed and water, and housing condition. One system may provide greater environmental control, while another may provide greater outdoor access. A trade-off could be that greater environmental control requires more infrastructure and waste management. The stronger choice would depend on animal observations, records, site conditions and the production context.

Prompt: Explain why a photograph of pigs and their housing is not enough to prove a welfare outcome.
Scaffold:

Identify the relevant ideas and evidence from this section.

Explain the relationship clearly, using a specific example and respecting the source boundary.

Appropriate response example: A photograph may show visible housing features or animal behaviour at one moment, but it cannot show health patterns, access to resources over time, monitoring, thermal comfort, biosecurity or management records. A welfare conclusion requires several animal-based and resource or management indicators collected across an appropriate period.
